topic.name: Thyroid Disorders
objectives: Interpret thyroid function tests (TSH, T4, T3) patterns
Recognize thyroid nodule workup and when to biopsy
Identify myxedema coma and thyroid storm — know when to refer

content_chunks.title: Why This Matters
content_chunks.content: Meet two patients. First: Linda, 45, exhausted, gained 20 lbs over 6 months, hair falling out, feels cold when everyone else is warm. Second: Rachel, 32, lost 15 lbs unintentionally, heart races, can't sleep, hands shake, always hot. Same organ — completely opposite problems. Thyroid disorders affect 20 million Americans (mostly women), and 60% don't know they have it. It's one of the easiest conditions to diagnose and treat — but you have to THINK of it first. Boards LOVE thyroid cases because the labs are so pattern-based.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Side-by-side silhouettes: LEFT (hypothyroid): sluggish, overweight, cold, tired. RIGHT (hyperthyroid): hyperactive, thin, sweaty, tremulous. Butterfly-shaped thyroid gland in center.

content_chunks.title: Thyroid Physiology: The Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Thyroid Axis
content_chunks.content:
**The Feedback Loop** (understand this = understand every lab pattern!):

**Hypothalamus** → releases **TRH** (thyrotropin-releasing hormone)
       ↓
**Pituitary** → releases **TSH** (thyroid-stimulating hormone)
       ↓
**Thyroid gland** → produces **T4** (thyroxine, inactive form) and **T3** (triiodothyronine, active form)
       ↓
**T4 → T3 in tissues** (by deiodinase enzymes) — T3 is 3-4x more potent!
       ↓
**Negative feedback**: High T4/T3 → suppresses TRH and TSH. Low T4/T3 → stimulates TRH and TSH.

**The Golden Rule of Thyroid Testing**:
• **TSH** is the **MOST sensitive test** — changes FIRST when thyroid is off
• Normal TSH = euthyroid (normal thyroid function) 95% of the time
• Abnormal TSH → check free T4 to determine: primary vs. secondary vs. subclinical

**Thyroid Lab Patterns (BOARD GOLD)**:

**Primary Hypothyroidism**: TSH ↑, Free T4 ↓
• Problem is IN the thyroid gland (most common!)

**Primary Hyperthyroidism**: TSH ↓, Free T4 ↑ (or T3 ↑)
• Problem is IN the thyroid gland (Graves, toxic nodule, thyroiditis)

**Subclinical Hypothyroidism**: TSH ↑, Free T4 NORMAL
• Compensated — thyroid is working harder to maintain normal T4

**Subclinical Hyperthyroidism**: TSH ↓, Free T4 NORMAL
• Mild excess T4 suppressing TSH

**Secondary (Central) Hypothyroidism**: TSH ↓ or INAPPROPRIATELY NORMAL, Free T4 ↓
• Problem is in PITUITARY or HYPOTHALAMUS (rare! brain tumor, Sheehan's)

**Sick Euthyroid Syndrome**: TSH usually normal or slightly ↓, T4/T3 low
• Non-thyroidal illness — don't treat the labs, treat the underlying illness!
content_chunks.mnemonic: **TSH tells the story**: TSH **H**igh → Thyroid is **L**ow (hypO). TSH **L**ow → Thyroid is **H**igh (hypER). **Same direction = primary problem in thyroid. Opposite direction = problem in pituitary.**
content_chunks.visual_desc: Feedback loop diagram: Hypothalamus → TRH → Pituitary → TSH → Thyroid → T4/T3 → (negative feedback arrows) back to hypothalamus/pituitary

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **Don't reflexively check T4 if TSH is normal** in a low-risk asymptomatic patient! TSH is the screening test — if it's normal (0.5-4.5 mIU/L), the patient is almost certainly euthyroid. Only check T4 if TSH is abnormal. Exception: if you suspect pituitary disease (TSH won't reflect true thyroid status).

mnemonics.mnemonic: **TSH tells the story**: TSH **H**igh → Thyroid is **L**ow (hypO). TSH **L**ow → Thyroid is **H**igh (hypER). **Same direction = primary problem in thyroid. Opposite direction = problem in pituitary.**

quick_checks.q: TSH is markedly elevated (12 mIU/L) and free T4 is low. What's the diagnosis?
quick_checks.explanation: **TSH high + T4 low = Primary hypothyroidism**. The thyroid isn't making enough T4, so pituitary cranks up TSH to compensate.

quick_checks.q: TSH is low (0.1 mIU/L) with normal free T4. What's the diagnosis?
quick_checks.explanation: **TSH low + normal T4 = Subclinical hyperthyroidism**. T4 is still normal but TSH is suppressed — early/mild hyperthyroidism. Often seen with small toxic nodules or early Graves.

lessons.title: 🥶 Hypothyroidism: When the Thyroid Slows Down

content_chunks.title: The Exhausted Patient
content_chunks.content: Linda is back. She's 45, BMI 32, always tired. Her skin is dry, hair thinning, nails brittle. She's constipated, feels cold all the time, and her periods are heavier. She says 'my brain is in a fog.' Physical exam: delayed deep tendon reflexes (hung-up reflex), mild periorbital puffiness, goiter (diffuse, firm). TSH = 18.9 mIU/L. Free T4 = 0.4 ng/dL. Classic primary hypothyroidism from Hashimoto thyroiditis — the most common cause in the US.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Clinical signs of hypothyroidism: periorbital puffiness, thinning lateral eyebrows (Queen Anne sign), dry skin, goiter, hung-up DTR (delayed relaxation phase)

content_chunks.title: Hypothyroidism: Causes, Symptoms, Diagnosis
content_chunks.content:
**Primary Hypothyroidism** (95% of cases):

**Most Common Causes**:
1. **Hashimoto thyroiditis** (autoimmune) — #1 cause in US
   • Anti-TPO antibodies + Anti-thyroglobulin antibodies
   • Often has goiter (but can be atrophic late-stage)
   • Associated with other autoimmune diseases (T1DM, celiac, pernicious anemia, Addison's)
2. **Iatrogenic** — post-thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine ablation, radiation, meds (lithium, amiodarone, interferon)
3. **Iodine deficiency** — #1 cause worldwide (not in US due to iodized salt)
4. **Postpartum thyroiditis** — transient hypothyroidism 3-6 months after delivery
5. **Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis** — Post-viral, painful thyroid, transient course

**Classic Symptoms** (the 'low metabolism' picture):
• **Fatigue**, weakness, lethargy
• **Weight gain** despite decreased appetite
• **Cold intolerance**
• **Constipation**
• **Dry skin**, brittle nails, **hair loss**
• **Heavy menstrual bleeding** (menorrhagia)
• **Brain fog**, slow thinking, depression
• **Hoarse voice**, puffy face (myxedema)
• **Myalgias**, arthralgias, carpal tunnel syndrome

**Physical Exam Findings**:
• **Delayed DTR relaxation** (hung-up reflex — most specific!)
• **Periorbital puffiness**
• **Goiter** (diffuse, firm, rubbery in Hashimoto)
• **Bradycardia**
• **Dry, cool skin**
• **Non-pitting edema** (myxedema)

**Diagnosis**:
• **TSH** — elevated (first sign — gets high before T4 drops)
• **Free T4** — low (confirms overt disease)
• **Anti-TPO antibodies** — positive in Hashimoto (NOT needed for diagnosis but confirms autoimmune cause)
• **No need for T3** (body converts T4 → T3; T3 is normal or low, not helpful for diagnosis)
content_chunks.visual_desc: Metabolic slowdown meter: All body systems slowed — brain (brain fog), heart (bradycardia), gut (constipation), skin (dry), metabolism (weight gain), reflexes (hung-up)

content_chunks.title: Levothyroxine: The Replacement Protocol
content_chunks.content:
**Levothyroxine (LT4)** = Treatment for hypothyroidism. **Synthetic T4** — body converts it to active T3.

**Starting Dose**:
• **Healthy adults <50, no CVD**: Start at **1.6 mcg/kg/day** (full replacement)
  → 75-100 mcg daily for most women
  → 100-150 mcg daily for most men
• **Age >50 or known CAD**: Start **LOW** — 25-50 mcg daily (titrate up every 4-6 weeks)
• **Mild hypothyroidism/TSH <10**: Start 25-50 mcg daily

**Administration** (crucial!):
⏰ Take on **empty stomach** with water ONLY
⏰ **Wait 30-60 minutes** before eating or drinking anything but water
⏰ **4-hour separation** from: calcium, iron, magnesium, fiber supplements
⏰ **4-hour separation** from: estrogen, antacids, sucralfate, orlistat, sevelamer
⏰ Take at **same time every day** (consistency!)

**Titration**:
• Adjust by **12.5-25 mcg** increments every **4-6 weeks**
• Target: TSH **0.5-2.5 mIU/L** (optimal = lower half of normal range)
• Recheck TSH **6-8 weeks after each dose change**
• Once stable → recheck TSH q6-12 months

**Pregnancy** (critical!):
• Pregnancy → **increase dose by 30-50%** (total T4 needs increase!)
• Check TSH as soon as pregnancy confirmed, then q4 weeks
• Goal TSH: <2.5 in first trimester, <3.0 in second/third

**When TSH doesn't normalize**:
1. **Non-adherence** (#1 cause! — 'I forget' or skip doses)
2. **Incorrect administration** (food, calcium, iron too close)
3. **Dose too low** (under-replacement)
4. **Malabsorption** (celiac, IBD, gastric bypass)
5. **Drug interactions** (estrogen, phenytoin, rifampin)
6. **Progressive disease** (worsening Hashimoto)
7. **Weight gain** (need higher dose per kg)
content_chunks.mnemonic: **Levothyroxine rules = 30-4-4**: **30** min before food, **4** hours from calcium/iron, **4**-6 week titration intervals
content_chunks.visual_desc: Timeline: Wake up → Take levothyroxine with water only → Wait 30 min → Eat breakfast → Wait 4 hours → Take calcium/iron supplements

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **Myxedema Coma** = severe decompensated hypothyroidism — MEDICAL EMERGENCY! Presents with: altered mental status, hypothermia (temp can be 85-90°F!), bradycardia, hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia. Triggered by: infection, cold, MI, sedation, stopping levothyroxine. **Treatment**: IV levothyroxine load (200-400 mcg IV) + stress-dose hydrocortisone (100 mg IV q8h) — because hypothyroidism can mask adrenal insufficiency, and giving T4 alone can precipitate adrenal crisis!

mnemonics.mnemonic: **Levothyroxine rules = 30-4-4**: **30** min before food, **4** hours from calcium/iron, **4**-6 week titration intervals

quick_checks.q: 55-year-old woman with hypothyroidism, starting levothyroxine. No known CAD. Best starting dose?
quick_checks.explanation: For healthy adults <50 without CVD, start at **full replacement** (~1.6 mcg/kg). For most women, that's 75-100 mcg daily. But for age >50, start lower (25-50 mcg). Since she's 55 (over 50), start lower at 25-50 mcg.

quick_checks.q: Patient on levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, TSH still 5.8. She takes it with breakfast. What's the most likely cause?
a: Incorrect administration (with food instead of empty stomach)
quick_checks.explanation: Taking levothyroxine **with food** dramatically reduces absorption. Must take on empty stomach with water, wait 30-60 min before eating. This is the #1 cause of 'refractory' hypothyroidism!
**Amiodarone** (antiarrhythmic, iodine-rich) can cause both hypo- and hyperthyroidism due to its iodine content. Monitor TSH before and q3-6 months on therapy!

lessons.title: 🔥 Hyperthyroidism: When the Thyroid is in Overdrive

content_chunks.title: The Wired Patient
content_chunks.content: Rachel, 32, comes in saying she can't stop losing weight. She's eating more but still dropping pounds. Her heart races, she feels anxious and jittery, and she's been sleeping 4 hours a night. She's always sweating. On exam: fine tremor, warm moist skin, tachycardia (HR 112), lid lag, and a diffuse goiter with a bruit. TSH = <0.01. Free T4 = 3.8 (high). This is classic **Graves disease** — the most common cause of hyperthyroidism.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Clinical signs: exophthalmos (bulging eyes), lid retraction, diffuse goiter, tachycardia, tremor, warm flushed skin

content_chunks.title: Hyperthyroidism: Causes, Symptoms, Diagnosis
content_chunks.content:
**Hyperthyroidism**: Excess thyroid hormone → hypermetabolic state.

**Most Common Causes**:

**1. Graves Disease** (60-80% of hyperthyroidism in US)
• **Autoimmune** — TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb) stimulate thyroid
• **F > M** (5:1), age 20-40
• **Triad**: Hyperthyroidism + **Goiter** (diffuse, bruit!) + **Ophthalmopathy**
  → Ophthalmopathy: exophthalmos, lid lag, lid retraction, periorbital edema
  → Can cause: proptosis, diplopia, optic nerve compression (urgent!)
• Pathognomonic: **Pretibial myxedema** (localized dermopathy)

**2. Toxic Multinodular Goiter (Plummer Disease)**
• Older patients (>60)
• Nodules autonomously produce T4
• NO ophthalmopathy (key difference from Graves!)
• More subtle symptoms (often just afib and weight loss in elderly)

**3. Thyroiditis** (transient hyperthyroidism — don't treat with ablation!)
• **Subacute (de Quervain)**: Post-viral, **painful** thyroid + fever, elevated ESR
• **Silent thyroiditis**: Painless, postpartum, lymphocytic
• **Phase 1**: Thyrotoxicosis (stored T4 leaks out) → **Phase 2**: Hypothyroidism → **Phase 3**: Return to normal

**4. Iatrogenic**: Taking too much levothyroxine (factitious thyrotoxicosis)
• Low TSH, LOW thyroglobulin (vs. high in endogenous causes!)

**Classic Symptoms** (the 'high metabolism' picture):
• **Weight loss** despite increased appetite
• **Heat intolerance**, excessive sweating
• **Palpitations**, tachycardia, atrial fibrillation
• **Tremor** (fine, outstretched hands)
• **Anxiety**, irritability, insomnia
• **Frequent bowel movements**
• **Oligomenorrhea** (light/absent periods)
• **Fatigue** (ironically! they're exhausted from being in overdrive)
• **Proximal muscle weakness** (difficulty climbing stairs)

**Physical Exam**:
• **Tachycardia**, AFib, **high pulse pressure** (wide gap between SBP and DBP)
• **Warm, moist skin**
• **Fine tremor**
• **Lid lag** (upper lid lags when looking down — von Graefe sign)
• **Goiter** (diffuse in Graves, nodular in toxic multinodular)
• **Bruit** over thyroid (increased blood flow in Graves)
• **Hyperreflexia**

**Diagnosis**:
• **TSH**: SUPPRESSED (<0.01-0.4)
• **Free T4**: Elevated (usually)
• **Free T3**: May be elevated even when T4 is normal (T3 toxicosis)
• **RAIU scan**: High uptake in Graves (diffuse), patchy in multinodular, low in thyroiditis
• **TRAb**: Positive in Graves
• **Thyroid ultrasound**: For nodule evaluation if indicated
content_chunks.mnemonic: **HypER = FAST**: **F**requent stools, **A**nxiety, **S**weating, **T**remor/tachycardia. **Mnemonic for Graves = GRR**: **G**oiter + **R**AIU high + **R**eceptor antibodies (TRAb)
content_chunks.visual_desc: Metabolic speedometer: All systems revved — heart (tachycardia/AFib), brain (anxiety/insomnia), gut (diarrhea), skin (sweating), eyes (exophthalmos), weight (loss)

content_chunks.title: Hyperthyroidism Treatment: Three Options
content_chunks.content:
**Three treatment options** — choice depends on age, severity, cause, pregnancy status:

**1️⃣ Antithyroid Drugs** (first-line for most young patients)

**Methimazole** (Tapazole) — PREFERRED (less toxicity)
• **Dosing**: Start 10-30 mg once daily, titrate to T4 normal (2-4 weeks)
• **Side effects**: Rash, arthralgia, cholestasis (rare), agranulocytosis (0.3-0.5%)
• **WARNING**: Agranulocytosis — give handout! If fever/sore throat → STOP, check CBC

**Propylthiouracil (PTU)** — SECOND-LINE (more toxic)
• Reserved for: **First trimester of pregnancy** (methimazole is teratogenic)
• Also for: Thyroid storm (blocks T4→T3 conversion)
• **Side effects**: Hepatotoxicity (black box warning!), agranulocytosis, ANCA vasculitis

**2️⃣ Radioactive Iodine (RAI)** — definitive treatment
• Indications: Recurrent hyperthyroidism, toxic nodule, older patients
• Contraindicated in: Pregnancy, breastfeeding, severe ophthalmopathy (can worsen!)
• After RAI: **95% become hypothyroid** (need lifetime levothyroxine)

**3️⃣ Thyroidectomy (Surgery)**
• Indications: Large goiter with compressive symptoms, suspicious nodules, pregnancy (2nd trimester), failed RAI, patient preference
• Must pretreat with methimazole + **SSKI** (Lugol's iodine) for 7-10 days pre-op to ↓ vascularity
• Risk: Recurrent laryngeal nerve damage, hypoparathyroidism, scar

**Before starting ANY treatment**:
• **Beta blocker** (propranolol 20-40 mg q6h, or atenolol) for symptom control
  → Reduces HR, tremor, anxiety within hours
  → Continue until T4/T3 normalize

**Thyroid Storm** (life-threatening!):
• Suspect when: Fever >102°F, HR >140, altered mental status, GI symptoms
• **Treatment**:
  → **Beta blocker** (propranolol IV or high-dose oral) — FIRST!
  → **PTU** 500-1000 mg load (blocks new hormone synthesis + T4→T3 conversion)
  → **SSKI** 5 drops q6h 1 hour after PTU (blocks release)
  → **Hydrocortisone** 100 mg IV q8h (supports adrenal function)
  → **Cooling**, **fluids**, **treat precipitating cause** (infection!)
content_chunks.visual_desc: Treatment decision tree: Young/want pregnancy → methimazole. Need definitive → RAI. Large goiter/compression → surgery. All start with beta blocker for symptom control.

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT)** — two types: **Type 1** (iodine excess in pre-existing Graves/nodule) → treat with methimazole. **Type 2** (destructive thyroiditis) → treat with corticosteroids. This is high-yield for boards! And a clinical challenge because amiodarone patients often have heart disease — hyperthyroidism worsens their arrhythmias.

quick_checks.q: 32-year-old woman with hyperthyroidism, diffuse goiter with bruit, and exophthalmos. Most likely diagnosis?
quick_checks.explanation: Hyperthyroidism + **diffuse goiter with bruit + ophthalmopathy (exophthalmos)** = classic **Graves disease**. Toxic multinodular goiter and thyroiditis don't have eye findings.

quick_checks.q: Which antithyroid drug should be used in the FIRST TRIMESTER of pregnancy?
quick_checks.explanation: **PTU** is preferred in the first trimester because methimazole is teratogenic (aplasia cutis, choanal atresia). Switch back to methimazole in 2nd/3rd trimester (PTU causes hepatotoxicity).

quick_checks.q: Patient with hyperthyroidism has fever 103°F, HR 150, confusion. Next step?
quick_checks.explanation: This is **thyroid storm** (fever + tachycardia + AMS). **BASH** protocol: Beta blocker FIRST (propranolol), Antithyroid drug (PTU), Saturated KI (SSKI), Hydrocortisone. This is a medical emergency!
